# Part 1 — Reproducible report and data description

## 1.1 Introduction

This report uses the provided **housing** dataset to fit and diagnose a linear model through NumPy matrix computation. The response variable is `price_thousands` (house price in thousands), and the three predictors are `size_sqft` (floor area), `bedrooms` (number of bedrooms), and `age_years` (age of the house). The purpose is to examine least-squares coefficients, fitted values, residuals, QR and singular-value decompositions, and numerical conditioning. Since the data are synthetic and observational in form, the findings describe associations, not causal effects.

## 1.2 Data inspection and validation


## 1.3 Reproducibility

All computations below run sequentially from the CSV, with no hidden notebook state, manually entered numerical findings, or absolute file paths. Results and tables are regenerated by Python each time Quarto executes this source document.

# Part 2 — Matrix setup and standardization

```{python}
#| label: matrix-setup
predictor_names = ["size_sqft", "bedrooms", "age_years"]
predictors = df[predictor_names].to_numpy(dtype=float)
y = df["price_thousands"].to_numpy(dtype=float)

# Standardizing the predictors
means = predictors.mean(axis=0)
sds = predictors.std(axis=0)

assert np.all(sds > 0)
Z = (predictors - means) / sds
X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(Z)), Z])
shape_table = pd.DataFrame({
    "Array": ["predictors", "Z", "X", "y"],
    "Shape": [str(v.shape) for v in (predictors, Z, X, y)]
})
print(shape_table.to_string(index=False))
print("\nStandardized column means:", Z.mean(axis=0))
print("Standardized column SDs:", Z.std(axis=0))
print("Design matrix rank:", np.linalg.matrix_rank(X))
print("Number of predictors excluding intercept:", X.shape[1] - 1)
assert np.allclose(Z.mean(axis=0), np.zeros(3))
assert np.allclose(Z.std(axis=0), np.ones(3))
```

The number of rows in `X` must equal the length of `y` so that every predictor row corresponds to one observed housing price. An intercept column of ones allows the fitted model to estimate a baseline price; with centered predictors, its coefficient equals the mean response. Standardization subtracts each predictor's mean and divides by its standard deviation, placing the three columns on comparable scales with mean approximately zero and standard deviation approximately one. NumPy broadcasting applies the three column means and standard deviations across all rows without an explicit Python loop.

# Part 3 — Least squares

```{python}
#| label: least-squares
beta_hat, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)
coefficient_names = ["Intercept"] + [f"Standardized {name}" for name in predictor_names]
coefficient_table = pd.DataFrame({
    "Term": coefficient_names,
    "Coefficient (thousands of dollars)": beta_hat
})
print(coefficient_table.to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.4f}"))
most_influential_idx = 1 + np.argmax(np.abs(beta_hat[1:]))
print("\nLargest absolute standardized coefficient:", coefficient_names[most_influential_idx])
fitted = X @ beta_hat
residuals = y - fitted
rmse = np.sqrt(np.mean(residuals ** 2))
print("Mean residual:", residuals.mean())
print("RMSE (thousands of dollars):", rmse)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
display(Markdown(
    f"The standardized predictor with the largest absolute coefficient is "
    f"**{predictor_names[most_influential_idx-1]}**, with coefficient "
    f"**{beta_hat[most_influential_idx]:.3f}** thousand dollars per one-standard-deviation increase, "
    "holding the other predictors fixed. "
    f"The intercept is **{beta_hat[0]:.3f}** thousand dollars and the "
    f"RMSE is **{rmse:.3f}** thousand dollars."
))
```

The matrix product `X @ beta_hat` gives the fitted price for each observation by combining its intercept and standardized predictor values with their estimated coefficients. The mean residual should be approximately zero because least squares with an intercept makes residuals orthogonal to the constant column. RMSE measures the typical size of the fitted model's errors on the response scale, in thousands of dollars. `X * beta_hat` multiplies elements using broadcasting and produces a matrix of per-term contributions, whereas `X @ beta_hat` sums those contributions for each row to give a one-dimensional vector of fitted values.

# Part 4 — QR, SVD, and conditioning

## QR decomposition

```{python}
#| label: qr
Q, R = np.linalg.qr(X)
print("Q shape:", Q.shape)
print("R shape:", R.shape)
print("Q @ R reconstructs X:", np.allclose(Q @ R, X))
print("Q.T @ Q is identity:", np.allclose(Q.T @ Q, np.eye(Q.shape[1])))
```

## Singular-value decomposition

```{python}
#| label: svd
U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(X, full_matrices=False)
X_reconstructed = U @ np.diag(s) @ Vt
print("U shape:", U.shape)
print("s shape:", s.shape)
print("Vt shape:", Vt.shape)
print("Singular values:", s)
print("SVD reconstructs X:", np.allclose(X_reconstructed, X))
```

## Rank and conditioning

```{python}
#| label: conditioning
X_raw = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(predictors)), predictors])
rank_X = np.linalg.matrix_rank(X)
cond_standardized = np.linalg.cond(X)
cond_raw = np.linalg.cond(X_raw)
print("Rank of standardized X:", rank_X)
print("Condition number of standardized X:", cond_standardized)
print("Condition number of raw X:", cond_raw)
print("Raw / standardized condition-number ratio:", cond_raw / cond_standardized)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
display(Markdown(
    f"The standardized matrix has rank **{rank_X}** out of **{X.shape[1]}** columns, "
    f"with condition number **{cond_standardized:.3f}**. "
    f"The unstandardized matrix has condition number **{cond_raw:.3f}**, "
    f"approximately **{cond_raw/cond_standardized:.1f} times** as large."
))
```

The check `Q @ R ≈ X` confirms that the QR factors reconstruct the original design matrix to numerical precision. The check `Q.T @ Q ≈ I` confirms that the columns of `Q` are orthonormal. Singular values measure the strength of the matrix in orthogonal directions; a very small singular value relative to the largest would indicate a weakly identified direction. A large condition number warns that some numerical computations may be sensitive to perturbations or rounding. The raw and standardized condition numbers differ substantially, with standardization improving the condition number in this dataset. This occurs because the raw predictors use very different measurement scales, especially square footage versus bedroom count, which affects the matrix's singular-value ratio. Because the standardized matrix is full rank and has a relatively modest condition number, it does not show evidence of severe near-redundancy among its predictors.

# Part 5 — Reproducibility and numerical-computing reflection

A computational report is credible only when another person can regenerate its results from the original data and the documented code. Clean execution matters because a notebook may appear correct even when its outputs depend on variables created by cells executed earlier in a different order. Running the report from a fresh session ensures that imports, data loading, transformations, model fitting, and diagnostics are performed in a transparent sequence. It also makes errors visible instead of allowing stale outputs to remain in the final document.

Reusable functions and code should not depend on hidden notebook state because hidden dependencies make the workflow difficult to inspect, test, and transfer to another computer. A function should receive the data or parameters it needs explicitly and return its result. For this assignment, the Quarto document builds the model matrices from the provided CSV rather than relying on values previously defined in an interactive session.

NumPy's `np.linalg.lstsq()` is preferable to manually calculating `(X.T @ X)^{-1} @ X.T @ y` because explicitly forming and inverting the normal-equations matrix can amplify numerical error. The condition number of `X.T @ X` is approximately the square of that of `X`, making ill-conditioning more serious. Least-squares solvers use more stable numerical methods and can handle rank-deficient designs more appropriately than direct inversion.

The QR and SVD reconstruction checks use `np.allclose()` rather than exact equality because floating-point arithmetic introduces tiny rounding differences. Mathematically equivalent matrices need not have exactly matching binary representations after multiple operations. A tolerance-based comparison tests whether those differences are negligible for the numerical task.

The condition-number comparison shows that numerical diagnostics are influenced by the units used to represent predictors. Standardization greatly reduces the condition number of this housing design matrix, so the raw value alone should not be interpreted as proof of strong multicollinearity. The standardized matrix's rank and singular values provide a more useful assessment of near-redundancy. In my final project, I will retain the practice of keeping raw data unchanged and generating the entire report from a single executable source using relative paths, with validation checks before analysis. This will make the final results easier to reproduce, audit, and update.
